question: How are multi-agent AI systems being used in software engineering, and what are their limitations?

sources.title: MetaGPT: Meta Programming for a Multi-Agent Collaborative Framework
sources.content: MetaGPT encodes standardized operating procedures into prompt sequences and assigns LLM agents human-like roles (product manager, architect, engineer, QA). Agents exchange structured documents rather than free chat, which the authors report reduces cascading hallucinations and produces more coherent solutions on collaborative software engineering benchmarks.

sources.title: ChatDev: Communicative Agents for Software Development
sources.content: ChatDev organises agents into a virtual software company that moves through design, coding and testing phases via chat chains. The paper notes that agents can still produce code that does not run or misses requirements, and uses a 'communicative dehallucination' step where an agent asks for missing details before answering.

sources.title: AutoGen: Enabling Next-Gen LLM Applications via Multi-Agent Conversation
sources.content: AutoGen is a framework in which customizable, conversable agents combine LLMs, tools and human input. Example applications include coding agents that write code, execute it, and use the execution results to fix errors, with optional human-in-the-loop oversight.

sources.title: SWE-bench: Can Language Models Resolve Real-World GitHub Issues?
sources.content: SWE-bench evaluates models on real GitHub issues from popular Python repositories, requiring a patch that makes the repository's tests pass. At publication, the best evaluated model resolved only a small fraction of issues, showing that real-world repository-level changes remain hard for language models.

sources.title: LangGraph documentation: multi-agent systems
sources.content: LangGraph describes multi-agent architectures (network, supervisor, hierarchical) where each agent is a node in a graph and control passes between them. It recommends splitting work across specialized agents when a single agent has too many tools or too much context to manage reliably.

analysis:
## Supported findings

- **Role specialization is the dominant pattern.** Systems assign agents distinct software-team roles such as product manager, architect, engineer and QA [S1], or organise them as a virtual company moving through design, coding and testing phases [S2].
- **Structured hand-offs reduce error propagation.** MetaGPT reports that exchanging structured documents instead of free-form chat reduces cascading hallucinations [S1].
- **Execution feedback loops are common.** Coding agents write code, run it and use the results to fix errors, optionally with a human in the loop [S3].
- **Specialization is a scaling strategy.** Splitting work across agents is recommended when one agent has too many tools or too much context [S5].

## Limitations and evidence gaps

- Generated code can fail to run or miss requirements [S2].
- On real GitHub issues, models resolved only a small fraction at the time SWE-bench was published [S4].
- The sources describe frameworks and research prototypes; none measure productivity in production teams.
fact_check:
- **SUPPORTED:** Systems assign agents software-team roles [S1][S2].
- **SUPPORTED:** Structured document exchange reduces cascading hallucinations, *as reported by the MetaGPT authors* [S1]. This is the authors' own evaluation, not independent replication.
- **SUPPORTED:** Agents use execution results to fix errors [S3].
- **SUPPORTED:** Splitting work across agents is recommended when one agent has too many tools or too much context [S5]. This is framework guidance, not an empirical result.
- **PARTIALLY SUPPORTED:** "Real-world changes remain hard" [S4]. The source supports this for its benchmark at publication time; results may have improved since and the sources do not say.
- **NOT ESTABLISHED:** Any claim about productivity gains in industry. No source measures this.
report:
# Multi-agent AI in software engineering

## Executive summary

Multi-agent systems for software engineering mostly mirror a human team: separate agents act as product manager, architect, engineer and tester, and hand work to each other in defined phases [S1][S2]. The strongest evidence shows two techniques that help: structured hand-offs between agents [S1] and loops where agents run code and fix it from the results [S3]. The evidence also shows clear limits: agents can produce code that does not run [S2], and resolving real GitHub issues was still hard for models at the time SWE-bench was published [S4].

## Key findings

1. **Role-based teams.** MetaGPT encodes standard operating procedures into roles [S1]; ChatDev runs a virtual software company through design, coding and testing [S2].
2. **Structure beats chatter.** Exchanging structured documents rather than free chat reduced cascading hallucinations in MetaGPT's own evaluation [S1].
3. **Execution feedback.** Frameworks like AutoGen let agents execute code and correct errors, with optional human oversight [S3].
4. **Why split at all.** Specialized agents are recommended when one agent would juggle too many tools or too much context [S5].

## Limitations and disagreements

- Reported gains come mostly from the systems' own authors [S1]; independent replication is not covered by these sources.
- Benchmark difficulty is time-sensitive: SWE-bench results reflect models at publication [S4].
- **Not established:** productivity impact in real engineering teams. None of the retrieved sources measure it.

## Conclusion

Multi-agent designs are a credible way to structure LLM coding work, especially with structured hand-offs and execution feedback, but the evidence here is from research prototypes and benchmarks, not production teams. Treat headline improvements as promising rather than proven.

## Sources

- [S1] [MetaGPT: Meta Programming for a Multi-Agent Collaborative Framework](https://arxiv.org/abs/2308.00352)
- [S2] [ChatDev: Communicative Agents for Software Development](https://arxiv.org/abs/2307.07924)
- [S3] [AutoGen: Enabling Next-Gen LLM Applications via Multi-Agent Conversation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2308.08155)
- [S4] [SWE-bench: Can Language Models Resolve Real-World GitHub Issues?](https://arxiv.org/abs/2310.06770)
- [S5] [LangGraph documentation: multi-agent systems](https://langchain-ai.github.io/langgraph/concepts/multi_agent/)
